leg: Europe → SFO, ~Nov 1–3 2026, party of 5 (4 adult-fare + one 8yo child), structure = 2 lie-flat business + 3 economy. LANE 4: cash and hybrid reality check.
summary: The lane-4 hypothesis is HALF TRUE and the half that is false is the dangerous half. Lie-flat business Europe→SFO in that window does exist at $1,886–$2,400/seat — but almost every fare in that band is Icelandair Saga via KEF, which has NO lie-flat seat on ANY aircraft in its fleet (2-2 recliner, confirmed). Strip those out and the cheapest VERIFIED flat bed is AMS→LHR→SFO on British Airways (Club Suite, 1-2-1, doors) at $2,164/seat — $4,328 for two, price holding exactly at true 2-pax occupancy on Nov 1, 2 AND 3. The same BA itinerary sells 3 economy seats for $1,539. So the all-cash 2-flat-beds-plus-3-economy structure, ONE flight, ONE day, is $5,867 and it is available right now with zero award-space risk. That is the number every points play has to beat. Why AMS and not LHR: identical BA metal on the LHR–SFO leg costs $3,159/seat if the ticket ORIGINATES at Heathrow ($6,318 for two) because UK Air Passenger Duty is levied on the journey's origin, not its connection point. Starting the ticket in Amsterdam legally avoids ~$1,000/seat of tax. That single structural choice is worth more than any transfer-partner arbitrage in this whole exercise. Three corrections to the brief's premises, all load-bearing. (1) Flying Blue is NOT 20k/35k/50k — that chart is dead. It is fully dynamic with no fixed chart; two independent sources put transatlantic floors at 25k/40k/60k and typical business near 72,000. Budget ~72k, not 50k. (2) The Amex Business Platinum 35% Pay-With-Points rebate NO LONGER applies to business class on any airline — Amex killed that Sept 18 2025. It now applies only to your selected airline (AA/AS/DL/B6/WN/UA), any cabin, via AmexTravel.com. On a BA or AF/KLM ticket the floor really is a flat 1.0 cpp. Residual lever: select Delta or American, then book a DL- or AA-marketed codeshare of this exact metal through Amex Travel to restore 1.54 cpp — plausible on paper, not verified bookable at these fares. (3) The "reprices the WHOLE party up" fear is structurally avoidable and should stop driving decisions. Flying Blue's engine won't mix cabins inside one PNR, but awards price one-way per booking — so you book 2 business as one PNR and 3 economy as a separate PNR on the SAME flight. The 5-seat saver-bucket problem never arises because you never ask for 5 seats in one bucket. Premium economy is a dead structure here, and the numbers are almost comic: real single-carrier BA World Traveller Plus from AMS is $1,903/seat versus $2,164 for the actual flat bed — $261 buys you a bed instead of a recliner. From CDG, PE ($2,150) is essentially the same price as business ($2,251). The cheap "$1,001/seat premium economy" fares are Condor+Alaska via FRA and SEA carrying a literal "Economy + Premium Economy" tag, meaning PE on one segment of a 2-stop 20-hour trip. Do not buy premium economy on this route. Upgrades are not a path: you cannot spend miles to upgrade an award ticket on essentially any program, and gate/check-in upgrades cannot be guaranteed for two adjacent seats for a family. Book the cabin you want outright. Verdict: the best USE of points is to spend them on the scarce expensive cabin and pay cash for the cheap one — 2 business on Flying Blue points (~144k miles for two seats displacing $4,328 = 3.0 cpp) plus 3 economy in cash at ~$513/seat, leaving ~$1,839 total cash out of pocket and ~380k of the 525k points still in the bank.

options.label: STRUCTURE 1 (RECOMMENDED, best risk-adjusted) — 2 business on POINTS + 3 economy on CASH, same BA flight ex-AMS
options.detail: Book AMS→LHR→SFO on British Airways (or the AF/KLM AMS/CDG→SFO nonstop if Flying Blue space is there). Put the two flat beds on an award — Flying Blue ~72,000 miles each is the realistic budget under dynamic pricing (floor 60k, range 55k–100k) — and simply BUY the three economy seats for cash at ~$513 each. This is the doctrinally correct allocation: points chase the scarce, expensive thing (a lie-flat seat worth $2,164) and cash buys the abundant, cheap thing (an economy seat worth $513). Redemption value on the business seats is ~3.0 cpp, the highest of any structure here, versus only ~2.05 cpp if you spend points on economy. It also fails gracefully: if business award space evaporates, you fall back to Structure 2 without having burned anything, because economy award space is the easy part and you never depended on it. Two separate PNRs on the same flight — required anyway, since no program will mix cabins in one booking.

options.label: UPGRADE PATHS — investigated and ruled out as a way to get two flat beds
options.detail: The brief asks whether they can book 5 economy awards and upgrade 2 later. The answer is essentially no, on every axis. MILES-UPGRADE-AN-AWARD: not permitted by any relevant program. United explicitly excludes tickets booked with miles from MileagePlus Upgrade Awards; American states mileage upgrade awards do not apply to award tickets; Alaska does not permit points upgrades at all; Turkish requires a PAID ticket. The general rule across the industry is that if you booked with miles you cannot spend more miles to move up. ELITE INSTRUMENTS: this is the one area that genuinely improved — from Feb 1 2026 United allows PlusPoints and Complimentary Premier Upgrades on award tickets, and AA systemwides work from an AAdvantage award in Main Cabin or PE. But neither United nor American is an Amex MR transfer partner, this family holds no status in either, and both instruments are waitlist-based, so they cannot deliver two confirmed adjacent flat beds for a family. GATE/CHECK-IN CASH UPGRADES: real on some carriers but structurally unsuitable here — they are offered at the airline's discretion, priced near the fare difference on deeply discounted economy fares, and cannot be guaranteed for two seats. You cannot plan a family trip around an upgrade that may not exist at the gate. CONCLUSION: book the business fare or the business award outright. There is no cheap back door.

leg: LANE 1 — Mixed-cabin mechanic (2 lie-flat business + 3 economy), Europe -> SFO, ~Nov 1-3 2026, 5 pax, 525k Amex MR

options.label: THE UNIVERSAL ANSWER: no program does 2J+3Y on one PNR — and that is GOOD NEWS
options.detail: Every one of the five programs prices a single award booking at ONE cabin for ALL passengers on it. The cabin selector is a search-level input, not a per-passenger input, on flyingblue.com, ba.com, iberia.com, virginatlantic.com and qatarairways.com alike. FlyerTalk's standing answer: you cannot put different-cabin passengers on the same PNR; the airline will only 'link'/cross-reference the two records (an agent note, not an operational join). Note the terminology trap: 'mixed cabin' in award jargon normally means one PASSENGER in different cabins on different SEGMENTS — that IS supported by AF/KLM and Iberia, and it prices at the highest cabin flown. That is a different animal from what you want. What you want is a SPLIT-PARTY booking: 2 pax on award A (business) + 3 pax on award B (economy), same flight, two PNRs. That is universally allowed and is the standard family tactic. CRUCIALLY, two PNRs is not a consolation prize — it is STRICTLY BETTER on the availability math, and the effect is largest on Flying Blue (see next row).

options.mixed_cabin_ok: NO on one PNR, for all 5 programs. YES as two PNRs on the same flight, for all 5 programs.
options.notes: TWO-PNR RISKS, priced honestly: (1) no protected connection between the records — but you are all on the SAME flight, so this risk is near-zero for you; (2) irregular-ops re-accommodation is handled independently, so a cancellation could rebook the 2 and the 3 onto different flights — this is the one real exposure; (3) separate cancellation/change fees per PNR (BA charges £35 each); (4) a split is generally irreversible. Mitigation: call and have the two records cross-referenced/associated, and add the same status number to both (a BA Gold/Silver on one record can then select seats free on the other).

options.label: (1) FLYING BLUE — the two-PNR split is the WHOLE game here, and it defeats the repricing problem
options.detail: YES, this is the crux, and your instinct is exactly right. Flying Blue has a fixed FLOOR price per route/cabin with dynamic pricing above it, and only a limited number of seats sell at the floor. The engine must price all passengers on one booking into the same inventory bucket, so a party of 5 gets quoted the higher tier FOR EVERYONE the moment saver inventory runs out — the documented failure mode is 'the minimum fare is 55,000 but that does not mean there are 4 seats at that price; often only 2, and then the fare goes up.' Booking 2+3 separately therefore changes the requirement from '5 saver seats in one bucket' to '2 saver business seats' AND '3 saver economy seats' — two much easier independent tests, in two DIFFERENT inventory buckets that do not compete with each other. Booking the business pair first does not consume economy saver seats. This is strictly better and you should not book 5 together.

summary: THE HEADLINE: "2 flat + 3 economy" is bookable on every one of the five programs — but on NONE of them as a single PNR. All five apply one cabin to the entire booking. You book two awards on the same flight: 2 pax business, 3 pax economy. This is the standard family tactic, not a compromise, and on Flying Blue it is STRICTLY BETTER than booking five together, exactly as you suspected: it changes the availability test from "5 saver seats in one bucket" to two independent easier tests in two non-competing buckets, so the documented whole-party repricing failure can no longer bite you. Do not let an agent build a single mixed-cabin record — that prices the entire ticket at the highest cabin flown, i.e. 5x business. RANKED: (1) QATAR AVIOS ON BA METAL, LHR-SFO nonstop — 172,000 Avios total (50k business / 24k economy per person, fixed distance chart, no peak dates), roughly HALF what the identical BA Club Suite costs through BA's own program, ~3.2 cpp. Single unverified variable: whether Qatar passes BA's uncapped surcharge through. Price it before transferring; the case rests entirely on that number, and I will not guess it. Only works as a nonstop — Qatar prices partner awards per segment, so any connection destroys it. (2) FLYING BLUE — 195,000 miles (60k/25k), dropping to ~176,000 with the 25%-off child fare for kids 2-11, or ~167,500 if the front pair is 1 adult + 1 kid. Position to AMSTERDAM, not Paris: KL's AMS-SFO carries $80-200 less cash per business seat than AF's CDG-SFO. (3) BRITISH AIRWAYS — 297,000 Avios and the cleanest mechanics: BA is the only program here that GUARANTEES 4 Club World + 8 economy reward seats per flight, so 2+3 sits inside the guaranteed allocation. Cash is £754 (~$1,010), not the feared four figures. (4) QATAR OWN METAL VIA DOHA — eliminate. (5) VIRGIN ATLANTIC — eliminate. THREE CORRECTIONS TO YOUR BRIEF: (a) Flying Blue's saver floor is NOT 20k/35k/50k — it devalued on 13 Jan 2025 to 25k/40k/60k, so your business seats are 10,000 miles more each than you have budgeted. (b) Qatar NO LONGER waives fuel surcharges — it reintroduced them as a distance-based "redemption fee" on 15 Sept 2024, roughly £125 per business sector. (c) Iberia MAD-SFO is confirmed dead for these dates (summer-only, not retained for the winter schedule that begins 25 Oct 2026), AND Iberia gives no discount on BA metal — the Avios level follows the OPERATING carrier, so Iberia Plus is BA pricing with BA surcharges. THE FREE WIN: Nov 1 2026 is a BA PEAK date; Nov 2 and Nov 3 are off-peak. Only three days in all of November 2026 are peak (the 1st, 21st, 29th) and you have picked one of them. Moving one day saves 38,500 Avios for the party at zero cost. THE CONSTRAINT THAT COULD KILL THE STRUCTURE: BA permits children aged 5-12 in a different cabin from the adult, but children UNDER 5 must travel with someone over 16. If any of your three is under 5, both adults cannot sit up front — you must run 1 adult + 1 kid in business and 1 adult + 2 kids in economy. THE FREE MONEY NOBODY QUOTES: UK APD exempts children under 16 travelling in the LOWEST cabin, so your 3 kids in BA economy pay £0 APD (~£306 saved). US flights are APD Band B (£102 economy / £244 business, measured to Washington DC, not to SFO) — several blogs wrongly quote the £253 Band C rate. The business APD premium is £142/seat, not double. LANE 2 LEAD WORTH CHASING: Iberia's cheap chart is only wasted because SFO is seasonal. MAD-LAX is year-round Iberia metal at 40,500 Avios off-peak business with ~$117 cash, on Iberia's own 1-2-1 A350. Two front seats for 81,000 Avios plus economy for three, then a separate LAX-SFO/SMF hop, may beat everything in this lane on both points and cash.
caveats: NO LIVE AWARD SPACE WAS VERIFIED IN THIS LANE. This lane answers the MECHANIC — can the structure be booked, and what does it cost — not the inventory. Every points figure here is a published or reconstructed chart rate, and every "status" is marked unknown except Iberia MAD-SFO (schedule-confirmed unavailable) and Virgin (eliminated on economics). Do not treat any total as bookable until a live search confirms 2 business + 3 economy saver seats on the same date. SPECIFIC SOFT NUMBERS, FLAGGED HONESTLY: (1) The Qatar-on-BA-metal cash is the single biggest unverified variable on the board and the entire case for the top-ranked option depends on it — I estimated $1,350 for the party from historical surcharge behaviour and did NOT quote it live. (2) Qatar's own-metal points (~112,500 business one-way) are RECONSTRUCTED by summing two legs; Qatar publishes no chart for its own flights, and the Flexi tier silently doubles the Saver rate when Saver space is gone. (3) The BA economy cash of £85/pax is internally inconsistent — it sits BELOW the £102 Band B APD, so it either predates the 1 Apr 2026 APD rise or already assumes the child exemption. Get a live ba.com quote. (4) Flying Blue cash is a range ($430-525 ex-CDG, $80-200 less ex-AMS) drawn from a verified June 2026 CDG-SEA data point, not from a CDG-SFO or AMS-SFO quote for your dates. (5) Qatar's winter 2026/27 SFO frequency (4x weekly) comes from an early schedule filing that the source itself warns "may shift before the season begins." (6) The BA peak/off-peak calendar was verified 2026-07-13 by a third party; BA publishes the definitive version on ba.com and has revised dates after publication — confirm Nov 2/3 on ba.com before booking. (7) Cash-alternative and cents-per-point figures assume ~$2,800 per one-way LHR-SFO business seat and ~$425 per economy seat, extrapolated from the $2,109-2,215 five-economy reference in the brief; if that reference was round-trip rather than one-way, every cpp figure here is roughly double what it should be and the rank order still holds but the absolute values do not. AIRCRAFT CAVEAT: BA still operates legacy 2-4-2 yin-yang Club World alongside the 1-2-1 Club Suite, and some AF 777s carry an older 2-2-2 business cabin. Both are lie-flat; neither is 1-2-1. Verify the specific tail before booking, because "business" does not guarantee direct aisle access on either carrier. OPERATIONAL RISK OF THE TWO-PNR STRUCTURE: if the flight cancels, the two records are re-accommodated INDEPENDENTLY and your family can be split onto different replacement flights. Cross-reference the PNRs by phone and put the same status number on both. This is the real cost of the split, and it is not zero.

options.label: #1 — ANA MILEAGE CLUB (Amex 1:1) on UNITED POLARIS or TAP metal — 50,000 miles per business seat one-way. THE LANE 2 WINNER, and it beats everything in Lane 1 for the business pair.
options.detail: Your brief said ANA is 'round-trip only, verify — if RT-only it is dead.' IT IS NO LONGER ROUND-TRIP ONLY. ANA began selling one-way partner (Star Alliance) awards for reservations/tickets issued on or after June 24, 2025, priced at exactly half the round-trip chart. The ANA partner chart for Zone 6 (North America) <-> Zone 7 (Europe/Russia 2) is 55,000 economy / 100,000 business / 165,000 first ROUND-TRIP — so one-way is 27,500 econ / 50,000 business. Two business seats = 100,000 Amex MR. That is cheaper than Aeroplan (75,000/seat), United (80-88,000/seat), Cathay (~89,000/seat) and Qantas (~104-108,000/seat) for the identical Star Alliance metal. THE SURCHARGE TRAP AND HOW TO DODGE IT: ANA DOES pass carrier-imposed YQ, and on Lufthansa Group metal it is savage — roughly $450/pp one-way ex-Germany, ~$800 per long-haul segment, and ~$2,000 round-trip Germany-US has been documented. Turkish carries ~$200-250/pp each way through ANA. BUT United, TAP Air Portugal, LOT, SAS, Air Canada and EVA pass NO fuel surcharges through ANA. So the play is ANA miles on UNITED POLARIS metal (nonstop to SFO from FRA, MUC, LHR, CDG, FCO, ZRH, DUB — United is the largest carrier in the SFO-Europe market with 32% of seats) or TAP A330neo LIS->SFO (year-round). Both are true 1-2-1 lie-flat. ALL-ANA SAME-FLIGHT VERSION: 2 x 50,000 + 3 x 27,500 = 182,500 MR of your 525,000, leaving ~342,500. summary:
HEADLINE: Lane 2 produces one genuine winner, and it is the program you flagged as probably dead. ANA IS NOT ROUND-TRIP-ONLY ANYMORE. ANA began selling one-way partner awards for tickets issued on/after June 24, 2025, at exactly half the round-trip chart. Europe<->North America partner business is 100,000 round-trip, so 50,000 one-way per seat. TWO LIE-FLAT BUSINESS SEATS = 100,000 AMEX MR. That undercuts Aeroplan (75,000/seat), United (80-88,000), Cathay (~111,000 after the 5:4 cut) and Qantas (~108,000) on the identical Star Alliance metal, and it is the cheapest business seat found anywhere in this lane by a wide margin.

THE CATCH IS SURCHARGES, AND IT IS AVOIDABLE. ANA passes carrier YQ, and on Lufthansa Group metal it is brutal (~$450/pp one-way ex-Germany, up to ~$2,000 round-trip Germany-US documented). THREE STRUCTURAL FINDINGS THAT REFRAME THE WHOLE LANE.

(1) YOUR FLYING BLUE NUMBERS ARE STALE — CORRECT THEM. The 20K/35K/50K standardized transatlantic saver was devalued on 13 Jan 2025 without announcement. Still very affordable against 525K, but budget correctly.

(2) "2 BUSINESS + 3 ECONOMY ON ONE PNR" DOES NOT EXIST — ANYWHERE. This is not a program quirk, it is how airline reservations are architected: one cabin per booking per direction. BA, AA, DL, UA all behave identically; FlyerTalk and Head for Points both report it cannot even be forced by phone. Flying Blue is the same. You will ALWAYS be booking two PNRs. Accept that and it becomes an ADVANTAGE, because (a) you can use two DIFFERENT programs for the two PNRs at zero cost, and (b) it defeats Flying Blue's worst mechanic — FB reprices the ENTIRE party to whatever tier holds all 5, so searching 5 people is the single most expensive thing you can do. Splitting 2+3 is literally the documented workaround. Your desired structure and the cheapest booking tactic are the same action.

(3) THE ROUTE WITH THE BEST BUSINESS AWARD AVAILABILITY IS LOCKED OUT OF YOUR POINTS STACK. SWISS ZRH-SFO is the consensus most-generous transatlantic releaser — routinely 4 business seats from schedule open, and uniquely it dumps West Coast business space within 2 weeks of departure. It is Star Alliance. Amex's only Star doors are Singapore KrisFlyer (144,000 RT Europe-NA business, round-trip chart, bad for a one-way) and ANA (round-trip only). The clean key is Aeroplan at ~70,000 one-way + ~CA$79 — a CHASE partner — and you hold 34,700 UR. Two SWISS business seats need 140,000 Aeroplan. THIS IS THE SINGLE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE GAP IN THE PLAN.

Norse is DOUBLE dead: its Premium cabin is a 43-inch-pitch RECLINER, not lie-flat, no business class sold at any price — and it dropped SFO after summer 2023. POSITIONING (your Q3), ANSWERED DIRECTLY. For the Flying Blue options (#1, #2, #3) positioning is a NON-ISSUE and costs nothing: any European city feeds AMS/CPH/CDG on the same award at the same mileage, on one ticket, with rebooking protection if the feeder misconnects. If the Dubrovnik-Ryanair constraint still applies at travel time, note it only binds you to Krakow / Vienna / London Stansted — none of which are SFO gateways — which is precisely why a program that carries the feeder free matters so much.

VERDICT: FLY HOME FROM AMSTERDAM. Every lane converged on it independently and the live fare data proves why. Primary play is KLM AMS→SFO nonstop on Flying Blue: 2 business at 60,000 miles each + 3 economy at 25,000 each = 195,000 of your 525,000 MR, with roughly $600-900 total cash for all five. TWO CORRECTIONS THAT CHANGE THE RANKING. (1) THE QATAR-AVIOS-ON-BA-METAL PLAY IS RETRACTED. Lane 1 ranked it #1 at "172,000 Avios, ~3.2 cpp, the best on the board," resting on a $1,350 cash figure it openly admitted was invented. I verified the chart (50,000 Avios for the 4,001-5,500 mile band is real and LHR-SFO at 5,354 mi qualifies) and then verified the thing that actually matters. BA's Reward Flight Saver is precisely the mechanism that trades MORE Avios for LESS cash, and it exists only inside BA's own program. Qatar has no RFS, so a Qatar-issued ticket on BA metal lands on the legacy structure — FrequentMiler's documented anchor is BA business at "50,000 Avios one-way and $950." Qatar's 50,000 matches that Avios level exactly. Run the marginal math: Qatar saves 125,000 Avios across the party but costs about $1,255 more cash, which values those Avios at 1.00 cent each — identical to simply cashing Membership Rewards out at the Amex Business Platinum floor. It is not a sweet spot, it is a wash. BA's own 99,000 + £249.50 is the better half of the same trade. (2) ANA'S 50,000 ONE-WAY IS NOT SAFE TO BUDGET. Lane 2 made it the winner by halving the 100,000 round-trip partner chart. Sources conflict on whether partner one-ways went live June 24 2025 or stayed round-trip-only until a NEW partner chart took effect May 19 2026 — a date no lane mentioned and which has already passed. One-ways are almost certainly bookable today under either reading, but the current chart's rates are unconfirmed and may not be a straight 50% split. Treat 50,000 as a number to verify on ana.co.jp, not a plan. ANA also requires every non-member traveler to be registered as an award user in advance, which can take up to two weeks — start that now if you want the option live.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT THAT OUTRANKS EVERY SEAT COMPARISON: no program on earth will sell 2 business + 3 economy on one PNR. That is reservation architecture, not a quirk, and it is confirmed across all five programs. You will always book two records. This is GOOD. It converts the availability test from "5 saver seats in one bucket" — which is what triggers Flying Blue's documented whole-party repricing — into two independent, much easier tests in two non-competing inventory pools. Your desired seating chart and the cheapest booking tactic are literally the same action. Never search 5 passengers. Search 2, then search 3. And never let an agent build a single mixed-cabin record: that prices the entire ticket at the highest cabin flown, i.e. five business fares.

SURCHARGES THAT ARE ACTUAL DEAL-BREAKERS, PER PERSON, ONE-WAY. UK Air Passenger Duty is the biggest and it is now PROVEN rather than argued: identical BA metal on the identical LHR-SFO leg costs $6,318 for two business seats when the ticket ORIGINATES at Heathrow versus $4,328 when it originates in Amsterdam. That is $995 per seat of pure tax structure, avoided by starting the ticket one country north. It is the single largest lever in this entire exercise and it is worth more than any transfer-partner arbitrage anyone found. Virgin Atlantic ex-UK Upper Class is £720 (about $975) per passenger — $1,950 for two, which is more cash than the entire five-person economy ticket, on top of 360,000 points; eliminate. Emirates is $800+ per business passenger plus a 5:4 Amex ratio (cut Sept 16 2025) plus a 24-hour eastward backtrack to fly west; eliminate. BA outside Reward Flight Saver, which includes any Qatar- or Iberia-issued ticket on BA metal, is about $950 per business seat. Air France ex-CDG runs $430-525 per business seat in French aviation taxes versus roughly $100-250 on KLM ex-AMS — this alone is why Amsterdam beats Paris, and the live fares agree ($4,328 AMS vs $4,474-4,503 CDG for the same two seats). Lufthansa Group metal booked through ANA is about $450 per passenger ex-Germany; if you go the ANA route, book United or TAP metal, which pass nothing through.

ONE TRAP WORTH REPEATING BECAUSE IT IS SEDUCTIVE AND WRONG: the $1,886-$2,400 fares that appear when you filter Google Flights to "business" are almost all Icelandair Saga via Keflavik, and Icelandair has NO lie-flat seat on ANY aircraft in its fleet. It is a 2-2 recliner with about 5 inches of recline. DUB at $3,771 for two is the most tempting of these and it is also 18 hours with two stops. If the requirement is that two adults sleep flat, none of these qualify at any price. Premium economy is separately dead: real BA World Traveller Plus ex-AMS is $1,903 per seat against $2,164 for the actual flat bed — $261 buys a bed instead of a recliner — and ex-CDG the gap collapses to $101.

THE ONE THING TO CHECK FIRST, BEFORE TRANSFERRING A SINGLE POINT: whether 2 KLM business saver seats actually price at or near 60,000 on AMS→SFO for Nov 1-3. The 25,000/40,000/60,000 figures are verified as current floors (they replaced 20k/35k/50k in an unannounced Jan 13 2025 devaluation, so the brief's numbers were one devaluation stale), but they are FLOORS under fully dynamic pricing, and the same seat routinely prices at two to three times the floor on busy dates. Sixty thousand is a hunt target, not a budget. Amex transfers are irreversible. Find the space first, then move the points — never the other way around.
